¶ '''attaste†''', ''v.'' [ME. ''ataste'', < OF. ''ataster'', taste, < ''a-'' (L. ''ad'') + ''taster'', taste: see ''taste''.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To taste. ''Chaucer.'' '''II.''' ''intrans.'' To taste (of). {{smaller block|Ye shullen ''ataste'' both thowe and shee
Of thilke water. {{right|''Lydgate.''}}}} '''atte†'''. Middle English assimilation of ''at the''. ''Chaucer.'' '''Attelabidæ''' (at-e-lab′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Attelabus'' + ''-idæ''.] A family of rhynchophorous beetles. See ''Attelabinæ''. '''Attelabinæ''' (at″e-la̤-bī′nē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Attelabus'' + ''-inæ''.] A subfamily of ''Curculionidæ'', typified by the genus ''Attelabus'', containing weevils with the abdomen alike in both sexes, the mandibles pincer-like, the elytra without a fold on the inner surface, and no labium. The group is sometimes raised to the rank of a family under the name ''Attelabidæ''. '''Attelabus''' (a-tel′a̤-bus), ''n.'' [L., < Gr. ἀττέλαβος, Ionic ἀττέλεβος, a kind of locust without wings.] A genus of weevils, typical of the family ''Attelabidæ''. {{smaller|''A. rhois'' is a reddish pubescent species with a short proboscis, infesting the hazel in the northeastern parts of the United States.}} '''attemper''' (a-tem′pėr), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''attempren'', ''atempren'', < OF. ''atemprer'', < L. ''attemperare'', fit, adjust, accommodate, < ''ad'', to, + ''temperare'', control, moderate, temper: see ''temper'', ''v.''] '''1.''' To reduce, modify, or moderate by mixture: as, to ''attemper'' spirits by diluting them with water. {{smaller block|Nobility ''attempers'' sovereignty. {{right|''Bacon.''}}}} '''2.''' To soften, mollify, or moderate: as, to ''attemper'' justice with clemency.
readings.c1s3:
{{right|''Barrow'', Math. Lectures, iv.}}
'''2.''' In ''brewing'' and ''distilling'', to regulate the temperature of, as the wort.

'''attemperate†''' (a-tem′pėr-āt), ''p. a.'' [< L. ''attemperatus'', pp.: see the verb.] '''1.''' Tempered; proportioned; suited.
{{smaller block|Hope must be proportioned and ''attemperate'' to the promise.
{{right|''Hammond'', Pract. Catechism.}}}}
'''2.''' Moderate; equable; mild: applied to climate.

'''attemperation''' (a-tem-pe̤-rā′sho̤n), ''n.'' [< ''attemperate'', ''v.''] '''1†.''' The act of attempering, regulating, adjusting, or accommodating. ''Bacon.''—'''2.''' The act of regulating the temperature of the wort in brewing and distilling.

'''attemperator''' (a-tem′pėr-ā-to̤r), ''n.'' [< ''attemperate'', ''v.'', + ''-or''.] In ''brewing'' and ''distilling'', a contrivance for regulating the temperature of the wort during the progress of fermentation.

'''attemperly†''', ''adv.'' See ''attemprely''.

'''attemperment''' (a-tem′pėr-ment), ''n.'' [< ''attemper'' + ''-ment''.] Same as ''attemperament''.

'''attempre†''', ''a.'' [ME., also ''atempre'', < OF. ''atempre'', pp. of ''atemprer'', attemper: see ''attemper''.] Temperate.
{{smaller block|''Attempre'' diete was all hire physike.
{{right|''Chaucer''.}}}}

'''attemprely†''', ''adv.'' [ME., also ''attemperly'', < ''attempre'' + ''-ly'', -ly<sup>2</sup>.] In a temperate manner. ''Chaucer.''

'''attempt''' (a-tempt′), ''v. t.'' [< OF. ''atempter'', ''attenter'', mod. F. ''attenter'' = Pr. ''attentar'' = Sp. ''atentar'' = Pg. ''attentar'' = It. ''attentare'', < L. ''attemptare'', more correctly ''attentare'', try, solicit, < ''ad'', to, + ''temptare'', more correctly ''tentare'', try:
readings.c2s3:
Foreign ''attempts'' against a state and kingdom
{{smaller block|<poem>Foreign ''attempts'' against a state and kingdom
Are seldom without some great friends at home.</poem>
{{right|''Ford'', Perkin Warbeck, i. 1.}}}}
'''3†.''' Temptation.
{{smaller block|<poem>To avoid
The ''attempt'' itself intended by our foe.
For he who tempts, though in vain, at least asperses
The tempted with dishonour foul. ''Milton'', P. L., ix. 295.</poem>}}
'''4.''' In ''law'', an act done in part execution of a design to commit a crime. ''Judge May.'' {{smaller|Mere solicitation or preparation, without a step taken toward the actual commission, is not a criminal ''attempt''.}} ='''Syn.''' Undertaking, effort, endeavor, enterprise, experiment.

'''attemptability''' (a-temp-ta-bil′i-ti), ''n.'' [< ''attemptable'': see ''-bility''.] '''1.''' The quality of being attemptable.—'''2.''' A thing that may be attempted. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Short way ahead of us it is all dim; an unwound skein of possibilities, of apprehensions, ''attemptabilities'', vague-looming hopes.
{{right|''Carlyle'', Heroes (1858), p. 35.}}}}

'''attemptable''' (a̤-temp′ta̤-bl), ''a.'' [< ''attempt'' + ''-able''.] Capable of being attempted, tried, or attacked; likely to yield to an attempt or attack.
{{smaller block|Less ''attemptible'' than any the rarest of our ladies in France.
{{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, i. 5.}}}}

'''attemptate†''' (a̤-temp′tāt), ''n.'' [< OF. ''attemptat'', mod. F. ''attentat'': see ''attentate''.] An attempt or endeavor; especially, a violent or criminal attempt or attack; assault; outrage.
{{smaller block|He called . . . for redress of the ''attemptates'' committed by the Greams. ''Strype'', Eccles. Mem., IV. 364. (''N. E. D.'')}}

'''attempt''' (a-tempt′), ''v. t.''   [< OF. ''atempter'', ''attenter'', mod. F. ''attenter'' = Pr. ''attentar'' = Sp. ''atentar'' = Pg. ''attentar'' = It. ''attentare'', < L. ''attemptare'', more correctly ''attentare'', try, solicit, < ''ad'', to, + ''temptare'', more correctly ''tentare'', try: see ''tempt''.]   '''1.''' To make an effort to effect or do; endeavor to perform; undertake; essay: as, to ''attempt'' a bold flight. {{smaller block|The wise and prudent conquer difficulties by daring to ''attempt'' them. {{right|''Rowe.''}}}} {{smaller block|Something ''attempted'', something done, Has earned a night’s repose. {{right|''Longfellow'', Village Blacksmith.}}}} '''2.''' To venture upon: as, to ''attempt'' the sea.—'''3†.''' To make trial of; prove; test: as, “well-''attempted'' plate,” ''Fairfax.''—'''4†.''' To try with afflictions.   ''Jer. Taylor.''—'''5†.''' To endeavor to obtain or attract. {{smaller block|This man of thine ''attempts'' her love. {{right|''Shak.'', T. of A., i. 1.}}}} '''6.''' To try to win or seduce; tempt; entice. {{smaller block|He will never . . . ''attempt'' us again. {{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., iv. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|It made the laughter of an afternoon, That Vivien should ''attempt'' the blameless king. {{right|''Tennyson'', Merlin and Vivien.}}}} '''7.''' To attack; make an effort against; assail: as, to ''attempt'' the enemy’s camp; to ''attempt'' a person’s life. {{smaller block|Muster Our soldiers up; we’ll stand upon our guard; For we shall be ''attempted''. {{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Thierry and Theodoret, i. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|Calumny never dared to suspect her morals, or ''attempt'' her character. {{right|''Goldsmith'', The Bee, No. 3.}}}} {{smaller|='''Syn. 1.''' ''Attempt'', ''Essay'', ''Undertake'', ''Endeavor'', ''Strive'', ''Struggle'', seek, aim. The italicized words agree in expressing the beginning of a task, physical or intellectual, which is difficult and often impossible. They are arranged in the order of strength. ''Attempt'' is to try with some effort. ''Essay'' is sometimes to try in order to see if a thing can be done or attained, and sometimes simply to attempt: as, “which the Egyptians ''assaying'' to do were drowned,” Heb. xi. 29. ''Undertake'' is, literally, to take a task upon one’s self, perhaps formally, and hence to go about a task with care and effort. ''Endeavor'' is to try with more earnestness, labor, or exertion. ''Strive'' is to work hard and earnestly, doing one’s best. ''Struggle'' is to tax one’s powers to the extent of fatigue, pain, or exhaustion. The first three words are more appropriate for a single effort, the other three for continuous or continual efforts.}} {{smaller block|None are very violent against it [writing plays in verse] but those who either have not ''attempted'' it, or who have succeeded ill in their attempt. {{right|''Dryden'', Ded. of Ess. on Dram. Poesy.}}}} {{smaller block|Instinct led him [Tennyson] to construct his machinery before ''essaying'' to build. {{right|''Stedman'', Vict. Poets, p. 155.}}}} {{smaller block|I will . . . ''undertake'' one of Hercules’ labours. {{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, ii. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|In what I did ''endeavour'', it is no vanity to say, I have succeeded. {{right|''Dryden'', Annus Mirabilis.}}}} {{smaller block|A certain truth possesses us, which we in all ways ''strive'' to utter. {{right|''Emerson'', Clubs.}}}} {{smaller block|O limed soul, that, ''struggling'' to be free, Art more engag’d! {{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 3.}}}} '''attempt''' (a-tempt′), ''n.''   [< ''attempt'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' A putting forth of effort in the performance or accomplishment of that which is difficult or uncertain; essay, trial, or endeavor; effort. {{smaller block|The ''attempt'', and not the deed, Confounds us. {{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, ii. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|By his blindness maim’d for high ''attempts''. {{right|''Milton'', S. A., l. 1221.}}}} '''2.''' An effort to accomplish something by force or violence; an attack or assault: as, an ''attempt'' upon one’s life. Foreign ''attempts'' against a state and kingdom {{smaller block|Foreign ''attempts'' against a state and kingdom Are seldom without some great friends at home. {{right|''Ford'', Perkin Warbeck, i. 1.}}}} '''3†.''' Temptation. {{smaller block|To avoid The ''attempt'' itself intended by our foe. For he who tempts, though in vain, at least asperses The tempted with dishonour foul. ''Milton'', P. L., ix. 295.}} '''4.''' In ''law'', an act done in part execution of a design to commit a crime.   ''Judge May.'' {{smaller|Mere solicitation or preparation, without a step taken toward the actual commission, is not a criminal ''attempt''.}} ='''Syn.''' Undertaking, effort, endeavor, enterprise, experiment. '''attemptability''' (a-temp-ta-bil′i-ti), ''n.''   [< ''attemptable'': see ''-bility''.]   '''1.''' The quality of being attemptable.—'''2.''' A thing that may be attempted. [Rare.] {{smaller block|Short way ahead of us it is all dim; an unwound skein of possibilities, of apprehensions, ''attemptabilities'', vague-looming hopes. {{right|''Carlyle'', Heroes (1858), p. 35.}}}} '''attemptable''' (a̤-temp′ta̤-bl), ''a.''   [< ''attempt'' + ''-able''.]   Capable of being attempted, tried, or attacked; likely to yield to an attempt or attack. {{smaller block|Less ''attemptible'' than any the rarest of our ladies in France. {{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, i. 5.}}}} '''attemptate†''' (a̤-temp′tāt), ''n.''   [< OF. ''attemptat'', mod. F. ''attentat'': see ''attentate''.]   An attempt or endeavor; especially, a violent or criminal attempt or attack; assault; outrage. {{smaller block|He called . . . for redress of the ''attemptates'' committed by the Greams. {{right|''Strype'', Eccles. Mem., IV. 364. (''N. E. D.'')}}}} {{smaller block|For the better defense of his highness’s loving subjects in the same shires in case of any invasion or other ''attemptate'' by foreign enemies. {{right|''Somerset'', quoted in Dixon’s Hist. Church of Eng., xv., note.}}}} '''attempter''' (a-temp′tėr), ''n.'' '''1.''' One who attempts, tries, or endeavors.—'''2.''' One who attacks or assails; an assailant. {{smaller block|Against the ''attempter'' of thy Father’s throne. {{right|''Milton'', P. R., iv. 603.}}}} '''3†.''' A tempter.   ''Milton.'' '''attemptive''' (a-temp′tiv), ''a.''   [< ''attempt'' + ''-ive''.]   Ready to attempt; enterprising; venturous.   ''Daniel.'' '''attend''' (a-tend′), ''v.''   [< OF. ''atendre'', F. ''attendre'', wait, reflex. expect, = Sp. ''atender'' = Pg. ''attender'' = It. ''attendere'', < L. ''attendere'', stretch toward, give heed to, < ''ad'', to, + ''tendere'', stretch: see ''tend'', and cf. ''attempt''.]   I. ''trans.'' '''1.''' To fix the mind upon; listen to; have regard or pay heed to; consider. [Archaic. See II., 1.] {{smaller block|The diligent pilot . . . doth not ''attend'' the unskilful words of a passenger. {{right|''Sir P. Sidney.''}}}} {{smaller block|The crow doth sing as sweetly as the lark When neither is ''attended''. {{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., v. 1.}} Their hunger thus appeased, their care ''attends'' The doubtful fortune of their absent friends. {{right|''Dryden.''}}}} '''2.''' To accompany or be present with, as a companion, minister, or servant, or for the fulfilment of any duty; wait upon. {{smaller block|The fift had charge sick persons to ''attend''. {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. x. 41.}}}} {{smaller block|Let one ''attend'' him with a silver bason. {{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., Ind., i.}}}} {{smaller block|You shall have men and horses to ''attend'' you,}} {{smaller block|And money in your purse. {{right|''Fletcher'', Rule a Wife, ii. 3.}}}} '''3.''' To be present at or in for purposes of duty, business, curiosity, pleasure, etc.: as, to ''attend'' a meeting.—'''4.''' To accompany or follow in immediate sequence, especially with a causal connection: said of things: as, a cold ''attended'' with fever; a measure ''attended'' with bad results. {{smaller block|A correspondent revolution in things will ''attend'' the influx of the spirit. {{right|''Emerson'', Nature.}}}} '''5†.''' To wait or stay for; expect, as a person or an event. {{smaller block|Thy intercepter, . . . bloody as the hunter, ''attends'' thee at the orchard end. {{right|''Shak.'', T. N., iii. 4.}}}} {{smaller block|The trumpets, next the gate, in order plac’d, ''Attend'' the sign to sound the martial blast. {{right|''Dryden'', Pal. and Arc., l. 1741.}}}} '''6†.''' To be in store for; await. {{smaller block|The state that ''attends'' all men after this. {{right|''Locke.''}}}} {{smaller block|One fate ''attends'' us, and one common grave. {{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Lucretius, iii. 304.}}}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To give attention; pay regard or heed: followed by ''to:'' as, my son, ''attend to'' my words. {{smaller block|''Attend to'' the voice of my supplications. {{right|Ps. lxxxvi. 6.}}}} {{smaller block|It will be sufficient for me if I discover many Beauties or Imperfections which others have not ''attended to.'' {{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 262.}}}} '''2.''' To be present, in pursuance of duty, business, or pleasure; especially, act as an attendant: absolutely, or with ''on'' or ''upon'', or ''at:'' as, who ''attends'' here? to ''attend upon'' a committee; to ''attend at'' such a church. Hence—'''3.''' To fix the mind in worship: with ''on'' or ''upon.'' {{smaller block|That ye may ''attend upon'' the Lord without distraction. {{right|1 Cor. vii. 35.}}}} '''4.''' To be consequent; wait: with ''on'' or ''upon''. {{smaller block|It is good that a certain portion of disgrace should constantly ''attend on'' certain bad actions. {{right|''Macaulay'', Moore’s Byron.}}}} '''5†.''' To stay; wait; delay. {{smaller block|For this perfection she must yet ''attend'', Till to her Maker she espoused be. {{right|''Sir J. Davies'', Immortal. of Soul.}}}} '''attend†''' (a̤-tend′), ''n.''   [< ''attend'', ''v.'']   Attendance. {{smaller block|Stars have made your fortunes climb so high, To give ''attend'' on Rasni’s excellence. {{right|''Greene and Lodge'', Looking Glass for Lond. and Eng.}}}} '''attendance''' (a̤-ten′dans), ''n.''   [< ME. ''attendaunce'', < OF. ''atendance'' = Pr. ''atendensa'', < ML. ''attendentia'', < L. ''attenden(t-)s'', ppr. of ''attendere'': see ''attend'' and ''-ance''.]   '''1.''' The act of attending or attending on. {{smaller|(''a'') The act of waiting on or serving; the state of being present for purposes of duty, business, pleasure, etc.; service; ministry.}} {{smaller block|No man gave ''attendance'' at the altar. {{right|Heb. vii. 13.}}}} {{smaller block|Lindamira, a lady whose . . . constant ''attendance'' at church three times a day had utterly defeated many malicious attacks upon her reputation. {{right|''Fielding'', Joseph Andrews.}}}} {{smaller block|The other, after many years’ ''attendance'' upon the duke, was now one of the bed-chamber to the prince. {{right|''Clarendon.''}}}} {{smaller|(''b''†) Attention; regard; careful application of mind.}} {{smaller block|Give ''attendance'' to reading. {{right|1 Tim. iv. 13.}}}} {{smaller|(''c''†) A waiting on, as in expectation.}}
